papers.title: Action-outcome coupling: a pre-investment feasibility audit for offline reinforcement learning in supply chain operations
papers.abstract: Prescriptive analytics initiatives in logistics, such as offline reinforcement learning and next-best-action systems, are often funded before anyone verifies that the available historical logs can support an improved decision policy. We formalise this pre-investment feasibility question via action-outcome coupling: a total-effect variance index measuring how much expected outcomes change with the logged action. Coupling provides an algorithm-independent upper bound on any policy's achievable value, expressed in monetary units per decision for both single-step and discounted sequential objectives. We also analyse the asymptotic false-licensing risk of an invalid workflow: fitting a value model and evaluating the model's greedy policy on the same data. The false-licence rate is driven mainly by the number of state cells over which selection is performed, rising from the nominal test level with one cell to near certainty with a few dozen, while overlap has a smaller effect. We then propose an audit that assigns logs to four tiers of decision support, separately for fixed and contextual policies, and returns an explicit stopping rationale. On a randomised e-commerce log, the audit endorses a fixed recommendation policy, certifying gains equal to 30 per cent of the theoretical ceiling; the remaining gap reflects bound looseness under an 80-action design. Two public logistics logs fail at different checkpoints: one because the target is an accounting identity of the action, and another because, with 27 clusters, estimated coupling stays below the design's detectability threshold even though a conservative offline learner certifies an improvement in 29 of 30 seeds.

papers.title: Inference after coding agents
papers.abstract: Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

papers.title: Multiply Robust Causal Mediation Analysis with Continuous Treatments
papers.abstract: In many applications, researchers are interested in the direct and indirect causal effects of a treatment or exposure on an outcome of interest. Mediation analysis offers a rigorous framework for identifying and estimating these causal effects. For binary treatments, efficient estimators for the direct and indirect effects are presented by Tchetgen Tchetgen and Shpitser (2012) based on the influence function of the parameter of interest. These estimators possess desirable properties such as multiple-robustness and asymptotic normality while allowing for slower than root-n rates of convergence for the nuisance parameters. However, in settings involving continuous treatments, these influence function-based estimators are not readily applicable without making strong parametric assumptions. In this work, utilizing a kernel smoothing approach, we propose an estimator suitable for settings with continuous treatments inspired by the influence function-based estimation strategy. Our proposed approach employs cross-fitting, relaxing the smoothness requirements on the nuisance functions and allowing them to be estimated at slower rates than the target parameter. Additionally, similar to influence function-based estimators, our proposed estimator is multiply robust and asymptotically normal, allowing for inference in settings where parametric assumptions may not be justified.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Tail Index Regression
papers.abstract: Motivated by the empirical observation of power-law distributions in the credits (e.g., ``likes'') of viral posts on social media, we introduce a high-dimensional tail index regression model and propose methods for estimation and inference of its parameters. First, we propose a regularized estimator, establish its consistency, and derive its convergence rate. Second, we construct a debiased version of the regularized estimator to facilitate inference and prove its asymptotic normality. Monte Carlo simulation studies corroborate our theoretical findings. We apply these methods (1) to the text analysis of viral posts on X (formerly Twitter) and (2) to the analysis of abnormally high health expenditures.

papers.title: The Online LSTM Prediction Models and The Term Structure of Predictions
papers.abstract: We examine and illustrate the properties of the Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) prediction models applied online to stationary inputs. We discuss the effects of: a) the network architecture that defines the admissible prediction functions, b) the objective function used to measure the prediction accuracy, and c) the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm. We also study the prediction optimality, the term structure of predictions, the filtered memory dynamics. We also introduce a set of diagnostic tools for memory-based prediction models that focus on the estimated dynamics of the hidden states.

papers.title: Estimation and Model Selection in Factor Models with Long Memory
papers.abstract: Panels in economics, finance and climate science are often driven by common components that differ in memory, such as common trends, cycles, or joint shocks. We study approximate factor models whose common factors are fractionally integrated with heterogeneous and unknown memory and develop the asymptotic theory of principal components for the panel in levels. Our theory builds on the eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix being ordered by memory asymptotically: a nonstationary factor group with memory $d>1/2$ generates eigenvalues of order $NT^{2d-1}$, whereas stationary factors generate eigenvalues of order $N$. Principal components estimate the factors consistently up to rotation, while adjacent factor groups are separated at a rate given by their memory gap. The information criteria of Bai and Ng remain consistent for the total number of factors, with their penalties acting as thresholds on eigenvalues that are asymptotically ordered by factor memory. When the nonstationary factors lose their variance advantage, estimation in levels remains consistent, whereas after differencing the factors can become undetectable. A Monte Carlo study shows that factor-number selection in levels tolerates more idiosyncratic noise than selection after first differencing. For monthly temperatures at $308$ European weather stations, our methods select two factors. The first is a persistent common warming factor. The estimated common component implies that 2021-2025 was $2.15^\circ\mathrm{C}$ warmer than 1960-1990, with the strongest warming in Eastern Europe. After first differencing, the criterion selects one factor, and loses regional heterogeneity as compared to the model in levels.

papers.title: Nested logit: model structure and normalisation
papers.abstract: Nested logit remains a widely used model, especially in applied work. However, there remains substantial confusion surrounding the existence of different versions of the model, different normalisations for the same version, and different software implementations. This paper argues that the labels in common use, RU1 and RU2, and the name non-normalised nested logit (NNNL) itself, have contributed to the confusion. The model is written in two forms: one in which utilities are divided by the structural parameter of the nest that contains them, which is consistent with utility maximisation by construction, and one without that division, known as NNNL. The difference between these forms is not one of normalisation. Normalising at the top or at the bottom gives the same model, and NNNL is itself normalised. What distinguishes the forms is whether the division is performed. In short, normalisation changes the units, whereas division changes the model. The undivided form coincides with the utility-consistent one only under specific conditions, and otherwise is consistent with utility maximisation only under utilities other than those specified, in which generic coefficients become nest-specific. The paper highlights that RU1 has been used for three different specifications, compares how widely used software packages normalise and report their parameters, and illustrates the consequences with calculated examples. The recommendation is that models be described by what they do, rather than by these labels.

papers.title: Long-Term Quantile Treatment Effects with Combined Experimental and Observational Data
papers.abstract: This paper studies the identification, estimation, and inference of long-term quantile treatment effects (LTQTEs) when short-term experimental data are supplemented with long-term observational data. Under a latent unconfoundedness framework, we establish identification of the LTQTE curve and derive the corresponding efficient influence functions. Building on these influence functions, we propose a semiparametrically efficient estimation procedure and develop a multiplier bootstrap method for uniform inference on the LTQTE curve, yielding valid simultaneous confidence bands over a continuum of quantile indices.

papers.title: Exact and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Multivariate Diffusions under High-Frequency Sampling
papers.abstract: We establish the asymptotic theory of the exact maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for discretely observed multivariate ergodic diffusions under high-frequency, long-span sampling, solving an open problem posed by \citet{YCW2019} and \citet{Li2013}. The drift may grow linearly, and the volatility is bounded away from zero and either bounded or proportional to $1+|x|$. When the sampling interval decays polynomially, the exact MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient, with rates $\sqrt{n\Delta_n}$ for drift and $\sqrt n$ for diffusion parameters. Under an additional condition on ergodic averages, and when the time span $n\Delta_n$ also grows polynomially, its moments converge as well. The proof never analyzes the exact likelihood directly: it shows that a closed-form density expansion of sufficiently high order is uniformly accurate in relative terms at every observed transition, so that the two log-likelihoods differ by $o_P(1)$ uniformly in the parameter. The same argument yields accuracy conditions under which an approximate likelihood is asymptotically equivalent to the exact one; in particular, the approximate MLE of Yang, Chen and Wan converges to the true parameter. For the delta-expansion estimator of fixed order $K\ge1$, we derive the leading bias explicitly. It shows that $n\Delta_n^{K+1}\to0$ cannot be weakened when the bias constant is nonzero, and that the bias falls on the drift parameters for even $K$ and on the diffusion parameters for odd $K$. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the predicted biases.

papers.title: One-Sided Randomization in Two-Sided Platform Experiments: Which Side Should be Randomized?
papers.abstract: Two-sided marketplace platforms often use randomized experiments to evaluate new features, raising the question of whether to randomize customers or listings. Randomizing the smaller (\emph{short}) side can reduce interference bias due to weaker competition, while randomizing the larger (\emph{long}) side provides a larger nominal sample, potentially reducing variance. On the surface, these competing considerations suggest a bias-variance trade-off in choosing which side to randomize. We investigate this trade-off in a two-sided marketplace with first-come, first-served (FCFS) booking and heterogeneous customer preferences, studying the bias and variance of difference-in-means estimators of the global average treatment effect. Our findings suggest that rather than a bias-variance tradeoff, in fact short-side randomization is generally preferable on {\em both} dimensions. We prove these results in an asymptotic regime where market imbalance increases. We establish conditions under which (1) short-side randomization eliminates first-order interference bias, while long-side randomization retains it; and (2) short-side randomization also achieves a variance rate of no larger asymptotic order than long-side randomization. The key insight is that although the long side contains more participants, the number of matches is constrained by the population on the short side, limiting the apparent variance advantage of randomizing a larger sample. Our conditions accommodate heterogeneous preferences and treatment effects and are satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice. Together, these findings support randomizing on the short side, despite the larger sample size available on the long side.

papers.title: Optimal Uniform Pricing for Multi-Interval Dispatch without Make-Whole Uplifts
papers.abstract: In a network with ramp-limited generators and inaccurate net-demand forecasts, practical rolling-window dispatch can drive locational marginal prices (LMPs) below generators' bid-in offers. In such cases, out-of-market (OOM) settlements are used to compensate generators and maintain dispatch-following incentives, but OOM can have negative consequences, including nontransparent real-time price signals, discriminatory compensation, and incentives for untruthful bidding. This paper presents an optimal uniform pricing rule that minimizes demand payments, eliminates OOM make-whole payments, preserves LMP-based congestion charges, and ensures revenue adequacy. We derive the proposed pricing rule in closed form and relate it to existing pricing schemes. Numerical comparisons demonstrate favorable generator profits and reduced price volatility. However, higher generator profits are accompanied by increased demand payments, reflecting the in-market, uniform allocation of ramping costs while preserving the LMP-based congestion charges widely used in real-time market settlements. The numerical results also show that, under LMP with OOM settlement, a price-taking generator has an incentive to inflate its offer, whereas this incentive is absent under the proposed pricing rule within the tested bid range.

papers.title: Difference-in-differences for mediation analysis using double machine learning
papers.abstract: We propose a difference-in-differences (DiD) framework with mediation for possibly multivalued discrete or continuous treatments and mediators, aimed at identifying the direct effect of the treatment on the outcome (net of effects operating through the mediator), the indirect effect via the mediator, and the joint effects of treatment and mediator, consistent with the framework of dynamic treatment effects. Identification relies on a conditional parallel trends assumption imposed on the mean potential outcome across treatment and mediator states, or (depending on the causal parameter) additionally on the mean potential outcomes and potential mediator distributions across treatment states. We propose ATET estimators for repeated cross sections and panel data within the double/debiased machine learning framework, which allows for data-driven control of covariates, and we establish their asymptotic normality under standard regularity conditions. We investigate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods in a simulation study and illustrate our approach in an empirical application to the US National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, estimating the direct effect of health care coverage on general health as well as the indirect effect operating through routine checkups.
